claimSlots.statement: In skilled healthy adult pitchers, critical shoulder kinetics occur shortly before maximum shoulder external rotation (arm cocking) and shortly after ball release (high compressive force).

claimSlots.statement: Evidence on shoulder range of motion as a predictor of injury in overhead athletes is uncertain and sport-specific: no significant pooled predictor in a 2018 meta-analysis; external rotation insufficiency associated with injury in professional pitchers (three pooled studies, caution) in a 2020 meta-analysis of prospective cohorts; range among several risk factors in a 2025 systematic review with inconsistent injury definitions.

lesson.title: Throwing and rotation
lesson.summary: Throwing puts the shoulder through fast, large rotations. Support throwers with strength and sensible workload, compare range over time, and know the warning signs.
objectives: Describe when shoulder loads peak during a pitch.
Describe the range differences pitchers' throwing shoulders typically show.
Explain why range is not a reliable injury screen on its own.
Know the warning signs in throwers, and refer young throwers with shoulder pain urgently.

blocks.content: This lesson gives a strength coach's view of the throwing shoulder. Throwing workload and return-to-throwing decisions belong to the athlete's sport coach and clinician.

In skilled adult pitchers, the largest shoulder loads come at two moments: shortly before the arm reaches its maximum external rotation during arm cocking, and shortly after ball release, when the shoulder must slow the arm down.

In professional baseball pitchers, the throwing shoulder typically has less internal rotation and more external rotation than the other shoulder. Part of that difference comes from a twist in the upper arm bone itself (humeral retroversion), not only from the soft tissues.
Range and injury risk: still uncertain

Whether shoulder range predicts injury is uncertain and depends on the sport. A 2018 meta-analysis found no range measure that significantly predicted injury in overhead athletes. A 2020 meta-analysis of prospective studies linked too little extra external rotation in the throwing arm to injury in professional pitchers, from three pooled studies, with a caution about the small number of studies, and found range screening may not identify risk in some other overhead sports. A 2025 review listed range among several risk factors, alongside reduced strength, previous pain or injury and training load.
So do not set out to make a thrower's two shoulders match, and do not treat one range number as a verdict. Compare total rotation between sides and over time, measured the same way.

content: Measure rotation the same way each time: same position, same time of day, before training.
Record both sides and the total (outward plus inward) for each.
Look for change across the season, not for a single number.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop the measurement if it hurts. Pain at rest or at night, pins and needles, or a new inability to lift the arm: urgent, today. Any thrower under 18 with shoulder pain: urgent, today; tell a parent or carer.

blocks.content: Build strength for the rotator cuff and the shoulder blade muscles, rotation strength through the trunk and hips, and the ability to slow the arm down. Progress one thing at a time, with the same stop rules as lesson 6.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Throwing workload, pitch counts and return-to-throwing decisions are for the athlete's sport coach and treating clinician. Your strength work supports that plan; it does not replace it. Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop throwing and shoulder loading for the session if the athlete has pain while throwing, loses velocity with pain, describes a "dead arm", or has numbness or tingling. Refer at the tier that matches (see "When to refer out"). A thrower under 18 with shoulder pain: urgent, an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 the same day, for referral to trauma and orthopaedics, with a parent or carer told.

blocks.content: Other rotational sports, such as racquet sports, swimming and combat sports, load the shoulder in related ways. Use the same approach: compare over time, build strength, and follow the stop rules.

content.prompt: In skilled adult pitchers, when are shoulder loads highest?
options: Just before maximum external rotation in arm cocking, and just after ball release
content.explanation: The largest shoulder loads occur shortly before maximum external rotation in arm cocking and shortly after ball release.

content.prompt: What range pattern does a professional pitcher's throwing shoulder typically show?
options: Less internal rotation and more external rotation than the other side
More internal rotation and less external rotation
content.explanation: The throwing shoulder typically shows less internal and more external rotation, partly from a bony twist in the upper arm bone.

content.prompt: Can shoulder range alone tell you which overhead athletes will be injured?
options: No: the evidence is uncertain and differs by sport
content.explanation: Syntheses disagree and differ by sport; range is one possible factor among several, not a reliable screen on its own.
